AI Policies for an AI Course

Most AI policies are about what you may not do. This one is mostly about what you will do, because this course is partly about AI: how it works, how it is changing digital research in the humanities, and above all how to use it to advance scholarship. Learning to use AI well is one of the main things you will take away from this course.

(A note on terms: on this page and in this course, “AI” is shorthand for generative AI, and in practice mostly for large language models, or LLMs, such as Claude, GPT, and Gemini: systems that produce text and code in response to prompts. Other kinds of AI exist; when we mean them, we will say so.)

Where This Course Comes From

This course has roots that go back well before generative AI existed. It descends from a course that David Birnbaum developed at Pitt, and some of its exercises, designed long before anyone could ask a chatbot for help, still earn their place.

But the world it was built for has changed. Most professional programmers now work with AI assistance: in Stack Overflow’s 2025 developer survey, 84% of respondents said they use or plan to use AI tools in their work, and about half of professional developers use them daily (Stack Overflow 2025). Some of what the original course asked of students, such as debugging long, complex programs by hand, is now something few working coders do unaided.

That makes the core ideas more important, not less. You cannot direct a tool well, or tell when it has gone wrong, unless you understand the logic of what you are asking it to do.

Our Stance: It Depends

Our stance toward AI is contextual. In many parts of this course you are expected to use AI, and to use it well. In other parts we will not use it at all. That is not because AI is bad. It is because understanding certain things without it will let you use it much better.

If you can (or cannot) use AI on something, that is by design. The default is that AI is allowed. When it is not, you will know: either the exercise is handwritten, so AI is out of the picture anyway, or we will say plainly that we are asking you not to use it. (Pitt’s Teaching Center describes a range of approaches to generative AI in courses; this course uses several of them, assignment by assignment.)

Pen and Paper

Counterintuitively, then, this course includes exercises done by hand, without a computer, let alone AI. These are isolated, in-class exercises on core concepts in coding and logic: What is a function? How does a computer think about paths? What is a for loop? We will work to understand each concept, make sure we can reproduce it, and demonstrate on paper that we have grasped it. The goal is to recognize the concept when you meet it, to understand it, and, yes, to ask AI to implement it for you in other contexts.

A quite reasonable reaction might be: “I will never have to do this in Real Life, so why on earth are we being tormented this way?” The invention of the calculator rendered long division obsolete… and yet you still memorized multiplication tables and carried out those decimals by hand in grade school. The calculator changed the purpose of those activities, making them a means to learning mathematical reasoning rather than an end in themselves. Coding is no different: if you want to tell AI what good code should do, rather than the other way around, you need to spend some time alone with pen, paper, and your own intellect.

There is research behind this, too. Studies of novice programmers have found that the ability to trace what a piece of code does, and to explain it in plain English, goes hand in hand with the ability to write it (Lister, Fidge, and Teague 2009). When AI does the writing, tracing and explaining are the skills you have left, and they are what tell you whether the writing is any good.

Responsibility

When you submit a piece of code, or use it in your project, you are responsible for it, even if AI did most of the actual coding. You answer for what it does, what it gets wrong, and what it breaks. Pitt’s own standard for AI use makes the same point: you are accountable for anything you produce with AI, and for verifying its accuracy.

In this course, that means you should be able to read the code you use, understand it, and explain it: what each part does, why it is there, and how you know it works.

Does that mean you need to sight-read every bit of syntax? Not necessarily. Ironically, AI can be very good at helping you decipher code, and we will teach you to do that better. And the stronger your independent ways of checking a result, the less weight falls on your reading of every nut and bolt. But you do need to understand the code you use at the level of its logic. Call it coding literacy.

Test the Output, Not the Story

Understanding the code is half the job. The other half is testing what it produces, rather than taking the AI’s word for it. This is easier said than done, and it will be a major focus of the course. One rule holds throughout: never accept the model’s own report of what it did as verification. Asking an AI “did that work?” and believing the answer is not checking. Professional developers have learned this the hard way: in the same 2025 survey, more developers said they distrust the accuracy of AI tools than said they trust it (Stack Overflow 2025).

To put it pithily: if it feels like magic when you get a cool result, that is not an acceptable outcome for this course. Magic is what a result looks like when you cannot say how it happened, or how you would know if it were wrong.

Showing Your Work: The AI Use Log

Whenever you use AI on course work, you keep an AI use log. Think of it as a laboratory notebook. For each task, record what you were trying to do, what you asked, what came back, how you tested it, and what you changed and why. The last two entries matter most; a log of prompts and outputs alone is just paperwork. The log is also how you disclose your AI use. Details and a template come with the first assignment that uses it.

The log records what you did. Your Worm Journal is where you reflect on what you learned: by hand, in ink, with no AI in the loop. Together they show us your understanding and your learning, not just your output, which is why output is not what this course grades (see (Un)Grading).

Tools

Everything AI-related in this course can be done with tools that cost you nothing:

  • GitHub Copilot in VS Code, for working directly with code. Copilot Free comes with VS Code, and verified students get the more capable Copilot Student plan at no cost through GitHub Education (GitHub Copilot plans). Verification can take a while, so apply in the first week (see Getting Set Up).
  • Claude for Education, Pitt’s university-provided Claude account, for a chat window and a second model to check the first against.

What you feed into these tools, especially copyrighted texts and archival images, raises questions of its own, covered on the course’s Copyright page.

How These Principles Apply to the Instructor

I hold myself to the same standards.

  • Grading and feedback: I will never, ever use AI for grading, or for feedback on your work. Not as a first pass, not as a suggestion, not at all. The same goes for the TAs.
  • Your work: I will never put student work into any tool, AI or otherwise, that Pitt has not approved for use with University data.
  • Course materials: I use AI in building this course, including some example code and some of the AI output you will be asked to critique. When the origin of something matters to an exercise, I will tell you.
  • Everywhere else: I use AI to design websites like this one, and constantly in my own research and work.
